extracted.intended_audience: FERC commissioners and staff, EPA policymakers, state regulators, and electric cooperative stakeholders
extracted.subtask_short: FERC comments on Clean Power Plan
extracted.subtask_description: Formal comments from the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) to FERC regarding the EPA's proposed Clean Power Plan (CPP), focusing on reliability, affordability, state implementation, and recommended modifications to EPA guidance. The document offers evaluations of CPP assumptions, timelines, and compliance mechanisms and prescribes changes to preserve reliability and protect rural electric cooperatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate interim goal reduction requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must eliminate the interim goal reduction requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim goals (2020-2029) undermine state authority, are unrealistic, create undue costs for consumers, and would undermine the reliability of electric service. States often cannot develop, gain legislative authorization for, and obtain EPA approval of SIPs in the timeframes EPA proposes (one year for SIP development; longer for regional plans). Building block measures (heat rate upgrades, new gas/renewable generation, energy efficiency programs) require years to engineer, permit, finance, and construct. Regional reliability studies (ERCOT, SPP, MISO) indicate interim goals would create reserve margin shortfalls and large costs. Therefore, FERC should urge EPA to eliminate interim goals entirely or provide much more time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a dynamic reliability safety valve
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must adopt a dynamic (as opposed to static) reliability safety valve that provides states the ongoing flexibility needed to ensure affordability and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The safety valve should operate as a relief mechanism to adjust or postpone emission targets in response to changing system conditions. It must be dynamic—allowing states to amend implementation plans and compliance goals as conditions change—rather than a one-time or rigid exception. Examples of circumstances warranting the safety valve include: major generator breakdowns, pipeline failures that interrupt fuel supply, transmission congestion, unexpected load growth, changes in market fundamentals or financing availability, regulatory delays (e.g., NRC), and other contingencies. The MATS (Mercury and Air Toxics Rule) safety valve — which allowed an extra year to implement without enforcement risk — is cited as precedent; any CPP valve should be similarly protective but dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide flexibility to extend the 2030 compliance deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must provide flexibility to extend the year 2030 compliance deadline (e.g., to at least year 2035) as required to preserve reliability and to prevent the stranding of assets or unreasonable rate increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even the 2030 final goal may force premature coal retirements in some states, harming reliability and consumers. Allowing extension of the final compliance date will mitigate stranded-asset risk and help maintain just and reasonable rates. The extension should be available where system conditions, permitting/constructing new resources, or other constraints make 2030 infeasible without undue reliability or economic impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay inside the fence (limit BSER to plant-level measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should stay 'inside the fence line' of affected coal-based power plants and focus on heat-rate improvements at the plants rather than relying on 'outside the fence' measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA contends EPA exceeded its statutory authority by relying on outside-the-fence BSER (e.g., shifting generation, demand-side measures, environmental dispatch). Staying inside the fence would focus on plant-specific upgrades (heat-rate improvements) that are within EPA's traditional authority and are less likely to create system-wide reliability and jurisdictional conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC review and modification of EPA models and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC should help EPA review and modify the models and assumptions EPA used to establish CO2 reduction targets for each state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's modeling assumptions (e.g., 6% coal heat-rate improvements, 70% NGCC utilization, broad adoption of environmental dispatch) likely overstate achievable outcomes. FERC's operational, legal, and economic expertise should be used to ensure state targets reflect realistic plant capabilities, market behavior, transmission constraints, and infrastructure timelines, thereby reducing infeasible state goals that would harm reliability and affordability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer SIP development timelines: five years (individual), seven years (multi-state)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide at least five years for individual states to develop implementation plans under Section 111(d), and provide states in multi-state plans with at least seven years to develop such plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposed one- to three-year deadlines for SIP development are unrealistic given state legislative schedules, required rulemakings, stakeholder processes, and multi-state negotiations. Longer statutory timelines would allow meaningful deliberation, permitting, financing, and implementation of infrastructure and program investments needed for compliance without jeopardizing reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: State discretion on which plants reduce generation under building block 2
rubrics_metrics.description: States should have the discretion to determine which plants would decrease generation as NGCC generation is increased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's alternative calculation that prioritizes reductions from coal-fired steam groups may be inappropriate for all states. States are better positioned to decide which specific units to reduce given local generation portfolios, remaining useful life, reliability needs, and contractual obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: States' prerogative on treatment of new NGCC emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment of emissions from new NGCC units that displace existing generation should be left to individual states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including or excluding new NGCC emissions in 111(d) plans has different effects depending on state goals and growth. States should retain discretion: in some states inclusion is counterintuitive; in others, especially with high load growth, inclusion may be necessary to meet goals. Uniform federal treatment would be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow crediting of mitigation actions concurrent with and before the plan
rubrics_metrics.description: States should be able to appropriately credit CO2 mitigation activities both concurrent with and backdated before the plan toward state goal accomplishment or allow appropriate adjustment of state goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, performance determinations did not hinge on a specific baseline date; allowing crediting/backdating recognizes earlier investments and avoids penalizing proactive programs. States should have mechanisms to count prior or concurrent reductions toward compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit a broad range of measures to be creditable (but not required as BSER)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures beyond the four building blocks—such as transmission and distribution efficiency improvements, partial CCS retrofits, biomass co-firing, and new NGCC units—are appropriate to include in a state plan to achieve CO2 emission reductions and should be creditable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA supports inclusion of any measure that mitigates CO2 as credit toward goal achievement. However, these measures should not be mandated as part of the federally defined BSER. States should be free to include them in plans with appropriate EM&V.

rubrics_metrics.name: State control over RE and demand-side EE crediting approach
rubrics_metrics.description: States should decide whether RE and demand-side EE are credited to particular affected EGUs (MWh crediting) or to the broader power pool/region; ensure no double counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA-proposed mechanisms can assume credits originate at particular EGUs, but alternative pool-based adjustments are valid. The choice affects accounting and double-counting risks; States should decide the approach provided reasonable assurance against double counting exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: EM&V protocols and guidance should be state-determined and EPA-accepting
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocols for evaluation, measurement, and verification (EM&V) of renewable energy and end-use energy efficiency for measuring compliance should be left to the states, and EPA should accept existing state EM&V methods (e.g., those used for RPS/EE programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States have existing stakeholder-negotiated protocols; forcing uniform federal EM&V would be costly and counterproductive. At a minimum, EPA should accept state-adopted EM&V methods without modification and limit any additional guidance to advisory materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting obligations should be left to states
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocols for reporting and potential reporting obligations for affected entities implementing RE and demand-side EE measures should be left to individual states to determine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States are best positioned to design reporting systems compatible with their programs and avoid duplicative burdens; EPA should not mandate uniform reporting beyond basic approvability criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance averaging time should equal performance period (12 months too short)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no apparent reason why the compliance averaging time cannot be equal to the performance period; a 12-month averaging time is too short for existing units that may need to compensate for unforeseen circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short averaging times can unfairly penalize units for temporary operational anomalies (weather, outages, dispatch changes). Allowing averaging equal to the performance period (or longer where appropriate) provides reasonable operational flexibility. For mass-based standards, EPA's three-year suggestion is more reasonable than a 12-month limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim goals and five-year alternative are not practicable (do not strengthen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate final goals (e.g., 2025 with 2020–2024 phase-in) and any strengthening of building block targets are not achievable for many states; the five-year alternative does not address the fundamental infeasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each building block is based on flawed/overly optimistic assumptions for many states. Shortening the timeline or strengthening targets would worsen reliability and affordability impacts. Therefore, options that tighten interim timelines/goals should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record retention not to exceed ten years
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no justification for record retention exceeding ten years for state plan records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA proposed a ten-year retention requirement; NRECA supports that or shorter but not longer retention periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require MWh-for-MWh fossil offsets for RE/EE additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals requiring states to eliminate a MWh of fossil fuel generation for each MWh of RE generation added or each MWh avoided through EE would make targets unattainable and create insurmountable reliability problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a strict offset rule would force premature baseload retirements and leave the system vulnerable during periods when intermittent resources underperform (wind/solar variability). It would exacerbate reliability risks rather than mitigate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: States should have flexibility in performance tracking (no mandatory 2025 submittal)
rubrics_metrics.description: States should be given flexibility to determine how to track performance and should not be forced into a second mandatory submittal (e.g., 2025) unless they choose to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While EPA proposes requiring tracking and potentially a 2025 re-submittal to ensure maintenance of final-goal performance, NRECA believes states can determine suitable periodic tracking and plan amendments without a prescriptive federal mid-course submittal requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for emission reductions affecting multiple states is an intra-state accounting issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an emission reduction becomes duplicative (and therefore cannot be used in a plan) if used as part of another state's demonstration should be resolved by the states to avoid double counting; EPA involvement only as last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-counting is an accounting problem best handled by cooperating states through agreed protocols; EPA should only intervene if states cannot resolve disputes. Upon resolution, state goals should be adjusted appropriately without voiding credited reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and infrastructure reviews should value fuel diversity and self-supply
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC should examine whether centralized markets appropriately value fuel diversity, fuel security, and long-term assets in a manner that properly incentivizes new investment and continued operation (including self-supply) by load-serving entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markets should not disadvantage self-supplied generation or long-term investments that support fuel diversity and reliability. FERC's review of market rules, transmission, and gas infrastructure should ensure continued incentives for diverse portfolios (coal/nuclear/gas/hydro/renewables) necessary for reliability, especially in rural cooperative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect existing baseload generation to preserve near-term reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve a diverse fuel mix and maintain existing coal plant capacity as baseload fuel, particularly in the near term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coal and nuclear demonstrated superior performance during events like the 2014 polar vortex. Premature removal of reliable baseload units risks reliability and increases exposure to gas-delivery problems and price volatility. Policy should avoid forcing premature retirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA additional guidance should be advisory not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Any additional technical resources or guidance EPA provides to States should be advisory in nature and not mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States vary in programs and governance; advisory guidance preserves state flexibility and avoids imposing one-size-fits-all requirements. EPA can provide helpful resources (e.g., guidance on multi-state plan development) but should leave final choices to States.
